content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper considers whether fairness in pre-training transfers to downstream tasks and how fairness can be achieved in unsupervised pre-training. The paper concludes that an imbalance in the data can lead to unfair pre-trained representation which cannot be readily fixed without sacrificing efficiency. The paper also proposes an unfairness metric applicable to self-supervising learning.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
(+) The paper proposes a three-stage training algorithm and a loss function. It seems to perform well on the cross-data set.

(-) The paper evaluates the proposed algorithm on only a single dataset and one fairness metric. The algorithm must be evaluated on several different fairness metrics including demographic parity and different variety of datasets. 

(-) To improve the readability of the paper, a simple example should be given regarding the algorithm.

(-) The paper does not seem to be missing ablation tests.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is generally clear, and it seems to be proposing an interesting metric that seems to be novel. The proposed algorithm seems to be simple, and the result should be reproducible.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper first investigates the unfairness transferred from contrastive pre-training to fine-tuning and shows that unfairness cannot be fixed by linear fair fine-tuning. To measure the unfairness of the pre-trained model, the paper proposes an unfairness metric that can be applicable to self-supervised learning and leverages that to guide the contrastive pre-training for fairness-aware representations.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
a)	This paper is well structured.

b)	The exploration of how pre-training unfairness results in downstream unfairness is novel and meaningful.

c)	The proposed feature-based fairness metric appears to be valid both in theory and experiments.

Weaknesses:
a)	Both Figures 1 and 2 are difficult to understand and require further organization.

b)	The proposed REAUG method mitigates the downstream average unfairness on 13 tasks. However, the method increases the unfairness risk on several tasks, such as Brown Hair and Wavy Hair with 1% FLFT data and LAFTR mitigation. For these tasks, the method seems unfair.

c)	In Table 1, some bold annotations make mistakes.

d)	The legend and description in Figure 5 are inconsistent and confusing.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work studies methods to measure and mitigate unfairness in self-supervised contrastive pre-training (e.g., SimCLR). For measurement, it first suggests the group-specific constrastive learning (CL) loss is not a reliable measure of pre-training fairness (Section 3.1). It then proposes Feature Disparity (Definition 3.1), a discrepancy metric based on the difference in the distribution of hidden-feature gradients between groups.  For mitigation method, it proposes ReAug, a masked training approach for CL that applies minority-group based global masking to all examples (Section 3.3), in order to encourage feature transfer from majority group to minority group. Authors empirically evaluated their method on face recognition datasets (CelebA, UTK, FairFace) with relatively baseline architectures (ResNet-18). The proposed approach appear to improve Feature Disparity without sacrificing accuracy.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
* Authors investigates the important problem of fairness in , self-supervised contrastive pretraining. 
* Authors proposed an interesting metric (Feature Disparity) to measure the feature discrepancy across groups.
* Authors conducted interesting qualitative analysis (Section 4.2) to showcase the upweighting effect of the proposed method, and the predictive power of the proposed metric.

Weakness:

* Lacking baseline comparison: The current experiment does not compare to baseline fair representation learning approaches. Therefore it is difficult to understand the efficacy of the proposed appraoch with respect to some simple baselines, e.g., simply reweight the CL loss during pretraining, or conduct adversarial training to prevent hidden representation from learning feature information (e.g., [Beutel et al (2017)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.00075)). These methods are not new and can all be adapted easily into CL context, how does the ReAug method compare? Please consider include relevant baselines in the experiments.

* Missing ablation study: In Section 3.3, authors discussed the advantage of global masking v.s. group-specific masking, please consider including relevant ablation studies regarding this design choice.

* Reliance on group information. The proposed approach seems to assume the group annotation for every example is known during pre-training time, which can be expensive or infeasible in practice. Furthermore, this may lead to problem if the group label does not cover all sources of bias in the dataset [Zhou et al (2021)](http://proceedings.mlr.press/v139/zhou21g.html). Please consider discuss such issues in the discussion / limitation section of the paper.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is well-structured and clearly written.

Section 2, Paragraph 3, " however could be expansive at practice." -> " however could be expensive in practice."
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper investigates the interesting problem of measuring and mitigating fairness in constrastive self-training. Authors proposed new metrics and a slightly complicated feature-masking strategy (ReAug). Empirical evaluation is conducted based on simple architecture and on standard academic benchmarks, with positive results. The paper currently does not compare to naive baselines (e.g., reweighting or adversarial training) in fair representation learning and lack some ablation study (e.g., masking strategy). As a result, it is difficult to understand the merit of the proposed approach (ReAug) compared to simple baselines, which prevents me from voting for acceptance.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors show that contrastive learning can result in biased feature representations and propose a new feature reweighing loss to alleviate this problem. In experiments, they show that their method improves fairness in multiple downstream tasks such as CelebA, FairFace, and UTKFace.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strenghts
=======
* Given the raise in importance of self-supervised learning algorithms, it is important to study the fairness of their representations in downstream tasks.
* The method is sound and it correlates with equalized odds
* In experiments, the authors show that the proposed method works even in combination with LAFTR and reweighting

Weaknesses
=========
* The authors did not provide the code and the details to reproduce their work are scarce. I encourage the authors to extend the appendix with more information to reproduce their work, possibly including a link to an anonymous github. Also, are the results in table 1 the mean of multiple runs? how reproducible are they?
* I found Section 3.3 difficult to read. I suggest the authors to send their work to a colleague to see if they found that section clear.
* The paper is heavily focused on SimCLR and it could improve by analyzing more unsupervised learning algorithms.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity
=====
* I found this work difficult to read. For example:

> It is easy to see that group-wise masking increases the dissimilarity of two different samples, i.e., $s^\tau(M^i_{A=0} \circ z_i...)$ if $(1−M^i )\circ z^i >0$

In this case, is $z_i$ a sample or a feature? 

> $\mathbb{P}(x) = \frac{1}{C} \sum^C_{i=1}\mathbb{I}(x^i)$? 

Is this the empirical distribution? is \mathbb{I} the indicator function?

> Eq. (7) has two factors: (1) discrimination: The gradient reflects the influence of the feature on local discrimination by the definition of the contrastive loss. (2) activation:

Could you point to which part of the equation is the discrimination and which one is the activation? (I know it is easy to deduce but it is easier if you explicitly state it).

* Could you better explain how to change from the second to the third term of equation 7?

* But the least clearly explained part to me is why to mask features from the unprivileged group in the first place. What I understand is that masking them makes the loss on unprivileged samples higher, which forces the remaining features to specialize for that group. However I got this intuition after reading the submission multiple times. I encourage you to go over the section, simplify it and make sure that the right points come across.

* There are some minor typos:
  - Section 1: "when combined with an efficient linearly fine-tuning" -> linear fine-tuning
  - Section 2:  "Thus, they propose **activate** feature collection, which however could be expansive at practice."
  - Section 3.2: quantitively -> quantitatively 
 
Quality
=====
* I am concerned about the technical quality given that the authors do not provide enough information to reproduce their research.

Novelty
======
* This work is novel to the best of my knowledge

Reproducibility
===========
* This is one of my main concerns (see above).
content.summary_of_the_review: This work is highly relevant for the current times, the method is sound, and the results are promising. I am concerned about the reproducibility and clarity of their explanations but I think that can be solved in the rebuttal. For the moment I recommend a score of weak reject.

content.title: Precautionary Unfairness in Self-Supervised Contrastive Pre-training
content.abstract:
Recently, self-supervised contrastive pre-training has become the de facto regime, that allows for efficient downstream fine-tuning. Meanwhile, its fairness issues are barely studied, though they have drawn great attention from the machine learning community,
where structured biases in data can lead to biased predictions against under-presented groups. Most existing fairness metrics and algorithms focus on supervised settings, e.g., based on disparities in prediction performance, and they become inapplicable in the absence of supervision. We are thus interested in the challenging question: how does the pre-training representation (un)fairness transfer to the downstream task (un)fairness, and can we define and pursue fairness in unsupervised pre-training? Firstly, we empirically show that imbalanced groups in the pre-training data indeed lead to unfairness in the pre-trained representations, and that cannot be easily fixed by fairness-aware fine-tuning without sacrificing efficiency. Secondly, motivated by the observation that the majority group of the pre-training data dominates the learned representations, we design the first unfairness metric that can be applicable to self-supervised learning, and leverage that to guide the contrastive pre-training for fairness-aware representations. Our experiments demonstrate that the underestimated representation disparities strike over 10% surges on the proposed metric and our algorithm improves 10 out of 13 tasks on the 1%-labeled CelebA dataset. Codes will be released upon acceptance.
